title: Gulf Oil Spill From Grounded Russian Tanker Reaches Oman Mainland, Rivals Exxon Valdez in Scale
excerpt: The oil slick from the sanctioned Caroline Bezengi now covers more than 2,000 square kilometers and threatens a marine nature reserve, with experts warning the spill could reach 50 million gallons if salvage efforts fail.
body:
• Oil from the grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi has reached the Omani mainland, the U.N.'s International Maritime Organization confirmed
  • The slick now covers more than 2,000 square kilometers, swelling more than 40 times since the beginning of August
  • The tanker carries an estimated 800,000 barrels of Russian crude and is under EU and UK sanctions as part of Russia's shadow fleet
  • Complex war- and sanctions-related rules are hampering cleanup, and the spill is being treated as an "act of war" rather than an accident

A Rapidly Expanding Disaster

A vast oil spill off the coast of Oman is quickly becoming one of the world's worst in years after spreading almost unchecked for weeks, according to international agencies, satellite imagery, and environmental groups.

https://x.com/AJENews/status/2087607674753929280

The slick from the Caroline Bezengi, a grounded tanker carrying Russian crude, reached the Omani mainland by Wednesday, the U.N.'s International Maritime Organization told Reuters. Oil spill specialist John Amos of SkyTruth, who reviewed satellite imagery obtained by Reuters, said the slick now covers an area of more than 2,000 square kilometers.

"A nightmare scenario is there's no adequate response to keep the worst from happening. The vessel would continue to break up under the steady onslaught of wind and waves and lose the entire cargo — that could be a spill upwards of 40 to 50 million gallons."

— John Amos, CEO of SkyTruth

How the Spill Unfolded

The Caroline Bezengi, carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of Russian oil, departed the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in April. The vessel, under European Union and UK sanctions for carrying Russian fuels, first reported difficulties off Yemen on June 8. Maritime sources said a blast appeared to have occurred aboard the ship.

No party has claimed an attack, but the vessel was navigating two separate wars on its journey from Russia to India — passing through the Suez Canal at the end of May before sailing past Yemen, where Iran-aligned Houthi militants have entered the wider U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict, according to Reuters.

The tanker ran aground on June 30 at Al-Qibliyyah Island, part of a marine nature reserve that includes the Hallaniyat Islands, putting endangered turtles, Arabian Sea humpback whales, and coral reefs at risk.

Cleanup Hampered by Sanctions and War

A web of complex war- and sanctions-related rules governing shipping and oil spills is hampering the response, according to insurers and analysts. The IOPC Funds, an intergovernmental agency dealing with tanker spill compensation, told Reuters it would not be involved in cleanup costs because the incident was being treated as an "act of war" rather than a simple accident.

The 25-year-old tanker is also not insured by any recognized Western insurance provider. Its owner, listed on shipping databases as Shanghai-based Rentoor Shipmanagement, could not be reached for comment.

The IMO said seasonal monsoon conditions had limited access to the tanker and delayed salvage operations. Oman said on Monday the slick covers almost 400 square kilometers and that it had used booms to contain the spread, but independent assessments put the area at several times that size.

Accelerating Spread

Environmental agencies say the spread has accelerated dramatically since the beginning of August. Greenpeace reported Tuesday that the affected area went from around 45 square kilometers by the end of July to 150 at the start of August, then quadrupled to 600 within two days.

Amos said the 2,000-square-kilometer assessment means the spill has swelled by more than 40 times since August began. At its full potential, the spill could rival the 1989 Exxon Valdez disaster in sheer size, he said.

"The longer we wait, the more damaged and decrepit that tanker gets, the more complicated and difficult and potentially dangerous that salvage operation is going to be," Amos warned.
nri_angle: The spill threatens a key shipping corridor between the Middle East and India, and could impact energy prices and marine ecosystems in a region with significant Indian maritime interests.
